title: Clearing the backlog: a $21 million Taser judgment, two prong-two immunity wins, and a canine release on a prone suspect
summary: No federal circuit, state high court, or United States Supreme Court decision on law enforcement use of force came down in the past seven days, and the Supreme Court is in summer recess until the first Monday in October. This week covers four 2026 decisions not previously reviewed. The Eleventh Circuit in Edwards v. Grubbs let stand $21 million against an Atlanta officer personally for a dart-mode Taser deployment, without warning, on a fleeing man above a steep embankment. The Fifth Circuit in Searles v. City of Houston and the Ninth Circuit in Foer v. City of Seattle granted qualified immunity on the clearly established prong only, leaving the merits of two fatal shootings undecided. A divided Fourth Circuit panel in Harold v. Hagan vacated immunity for a canine release on a prone, compliant burglary suspect, though a rehearing petition was pending. Across all four, the warning and the documented opportunity to comply is the fact courts reach for first.
coverage: The episode reported that no federal circuit, no notable state high court, and no United States Supreme Court decision on law enforcement use of force was issued in the seven days before September 5, 2026. The Supreme Court was in summer recess and does not convene for the new term until the first Monday in October.

All four cases in this brief are earlier 2026 decisions covered for the first time, not decisions from the coverage week. The current en banc posture of Harold v. Hagan could not be confirmed from a reliable source; a petition for rehearing and rehearing en banc was filed in May.

The statement that Officer Grubbs's wages are subject to garnishment comes from reporting after the decision, not from the opinion itself. Several case and officer names were spelled inconsistently in the source and are flagged in cautions below.
This brief was rebuilt from the episode originally published on September 5, 2026; it was not re-researched, so verify every citation against the opinion before relying on it.

sections.heading: Ninth Circuit
sections.note: No new Ninth Circuit force decision in the past seven days. The Ninth Circuit case below was filed May 7, 2026 and is covered for the first time because it matters directly to Washington State agencies and is the cleanest illustration of what a well-documented containment record buys an agency.

cases.name: Foer v. City of Seattle
cases.topic: Deadly force on an armed, fleeing suspect holding a child after a prolonged containment, qualified immunity on the clearly established prong
cases.caution: The source is a machine transcript that rendered the case name as Foer, Forre, Four, and 4-1 at different points; Foer is used here because it appears most often. The officer's name appears as both Zeck and Zech. The episode did not say whether the opinion is published. Confirm the citation, the spelling, and the publication status against the opinion before citing it.
cases.facts: Seattle officers responded to reports that Sean Foer had threatened the mother of his one-year-old daughter, violated a no-contact order, and fired a handgun in a public park. Foer fled while carrying the infant. Officers pursued him for more than 30 minutes, and the response escalated to include a helicopter and SWAT personnel. Foer ignored repeated police commands throughout. SWAT officers, including Officer Noah Zeck, eventually encountered Foer in a residential alley. Foer emerged from behind bushes, advancing, still holding his daughter in his arms. Zeck fired a single shot and killed him. The child was physically unharmed. Foer's handgun was recovered nearby. The family sued, and the district court granted summary judgment for Zeck.
cases.holding: The Ninth Circuit affirmed summary judgment for Officer Zeck. Even viewing the facts in the light most favorable to the plaintiffs, the court held that Zeck did not violate clearly established law. No precedent addressed a fleeing, likely armed suspect who had already fired a weapon, was holding a child, and had ignored commands for over half an hour. The decision rests on the second prong of qualified immunity. As in Searles v. City of Houston, the court declined to say whether the force was constitutional at all, which the episode described as now the dominant pattern in deadly force cases: the merits question in most of these encounters remains formally unanswered.
cases.notDecided: Whether the single shot was objectively reasonable under the Fourth Amendment. The court resolved the case on the clearly established prong only.
cases.inPractice: The 30 minutes of containment is evidence, not dead time. The record of every less lethal alternative attempted, every command ignored, and every opportunity to comply extended and refused is what made the final shot defensible. A prong-two win also means the tactical question is untouched; the court did not endorse the shot, it held that no earlier case clearly forbade it.
cases.trainIt: First, one shot. Zeck fired once with a one-year-old in physical contact with the target. That is a marksmanship and backdrop problem before it is a legal one. Agencies that put officers into hostage rescue adjacent scenarios owe them realistic training in precision shot placement with a non-combatant in contact, and an honest institutional conversation about when that shot is not available. Second, train officers and report reviewers to treat the containment phase as substantive narrative, not background. If officers do not write that phase down, the agency cannot spend it later. Third, do not read a prong-two win as a clearance; the merits remain open for the next case.

sections.heading: Supreme Court
sections.note: Nothing this week. The Supreme Court is in summer recess and does not convene for the new term until the first Monday in October. The episode described this as a structural gap in the calendar that opens every year between the end of June and the start of October, not a slow news cycle.

sections.heading: Other federal circuits
sections.note: No new circuit force decision in the past seven days. The three cases below are earlier 2026 decisions covered for the first time. Two of them, Edwards and Searles, come out of the same doctrinal door and land in opposite places; the contrast is the lesson.

cases.name: Edwards v. Grubbs
cases.topic: Dart-mode Taser without warning on a fleeing, unarmed suspect above a steep embankment, personal liability
cases.caution: The statement that the officer's wages are subject to garnishment comes from reporting after the decision, not from the opinion. The case is captioned in the name of Blassingame's representative; the transcript did not explain the Edwards caption further. Verify the citation and the dollar figures against the opinion. The episode did not say whether this opinion is published.
cases.facts: In July 2018, two Atlanta police officers encountered Jerry Blassingame, a 65-year-old homeless man, near a highway on-ramp. They had seen him receive money from a driver. When the officers approached, Blassingame ran. Officer John Grubbs pursued him on foot across traffic. Blassingame crossed a guardrail and started down a steep embankment toward the highway below. Grubbs fired his Taser in dart mode and struck Blassingame in the back. He gave no verbal warning first. Blassingame fell down the embankment and suffered catastrophic injuries, including a traumatic brain injury and quadriplegia. The case is captioned in the name of his representative. A jury returned $60 million against the City of Atlanta and $40 million against Grubbs individually. The district court set aside the verdict against the city, holding there was insufficient evidence of municipal liability, and reduced the punitive damages against Grubbs to $1 million.
cases.holding: The Eleventh Circuit affirmed what was left of the verdict. Grubbs was not entitled to qualified immunity. The court held that deploying a Taser in dart mode without warning against an unarmed, non-dangerous suspect who is fleeing on foot in a highly dangerous location is excessive force under clearly established law. The panel let stand $20 million in compensatory damages and $1 million in punitive damages against the officer personally, a total of $21 million against the officer, not the city. The episode called it the most financially consequential use of force decision of the year. Reporting after the decision indicates the officer's wages are subject to garnishment. The episode's analysis: Blassingame ran, and running was the whole of it. He was unarmed, the underlying conduct was minor, and nothing indicated he threatened anyone, so under Graham v. Connor the severity of the offense and the immediacy of the threat both cut against force. The episode described this as Tennessee v. Garner logic migrating into the less lethal space.
cases.dissent: Judge Newsom dissented on the clearly established prong. He would have held that the majority stretched existing precedent too far.
cases.inPractice: The case turns on the absence of a warning. A Taser warning is not a courtesy and not a de-escalation slogan; it is the single cheapest piece of legal protection available in a dart deployment, takes under two seconds, and its absence is what the Eleventh Circuit hung liability on. Dart mode causes neuromuscular incapacitation, and an incapacitated person does not catch himself, so the ground under the subject is part of the force decision. Fleeing is not dangerousness: under Graham, the severity of the offense and the immediacy of the threat are separate factors, and a suspect who is merely leaving does not satisfy the second one.
cases.trainIt: Three mechanical points. First, if policy says warn when feasible, training must define feasible narrowly so officers understand the default is to warn and the exception has to be articulated. Second, add a terrain assessment step to the Taser block that is as automatic as the arc display check: embankments, stairwells, elevated platforms, roadways, water, and moving traffic convert a less lethal option into a potentially lethal one. If the subject is above a drop, the Taser is not a less lethal option in that moment. Third, teach that flight alone does not carry a force decision when the subject is unarmed, the conduct is minor, and no one has been threatened. Tell officers about the $21 million and that it was entered against the officer personally; the municipal verdict was set aside.

cases.name: Searles v. City of Houston
cases.topic: Fatal shooting of a suspect with firearm warrants who turned with an object at his waistband, qualified immunity on the clearly established prong
cases.caution: The officer's name appears as both Prevett and Prevette in the source; Prevett is used because it appears first. Verify the spelling and the citation against the opinion. The episode did not say whether this opinion is published.
cases.facts: Jalen Randall was wanted on felony warrants, including firearm offenses. Houston officers attempted to arrest him and a vehicle pursuit followed. When the pursuit ended, Randall got out of the vehicle. He turned back toward the vehicle to retrieve a bag. He then turned again, holding an object near his waistband. Officer Prevett began yelling, show me your hands, and fired before he had finished saying it. Randall was killed. A firearm was later recovered inside the bag, not in Randall's hand. The estate and family sued for excessive force, along with supervisory and municipal claims. The district court granted summary judgment, finding the force objectively reasonable and, separately, that no clearly established law prohibited it.
cases.holding: The Fifth Circuit affirmed, but on the second prong only. The panel held that the plaintiffs failed to identify controlling authority, or a robust consensus of persuasive authority, with facts close enough to place the constitutional question beyond debate. The court did not hold that the shooting was reasonable. It held that no prior case told this officer clearly enough that it was not. That distinction is the whole ballgame. When a court resolves a case on prong two, it has answered the liability question and left the tactical question completely untouched. The episode tied this to a point made in a recent Lexipol column by Mike Ranalli: qualified immunity is not a training standard.
cases.notDecided: Whether the shooting was objectively reasonable under the Fourth Amendment. The Fifth Circuit left the district court's reasonableness finding untouched and decided only that the law was not clearly established.
cases.inPractice: Same doctrine as Edwards, opposite result. The lawfulness of the shooting does not depend on what was actually in the bag; it depends on what the officer reasonably perceived, and that perception has to be documented in specific sensory terms. A prong-two win is unstable ground: a decision that rests entirely on the absence of a factually similar precedent stops protecting the agency the moment such a precedent exists. Every prong-two win in a circuit is a warning shot, not a green light.
cases.trainIt: First, the command and fire interval. The officer started a command and fired before completing it. The Fifth Circuit did not condemn that, but no agency should be comfortable with it. If an officer has enough time and perceived safety margin to begin a verbal command, that is evidence there was at least some interval available for assessment; train officers to notice that interval and use it, because the next panel in the next circuit may treat the same interval as proof that a more measured response was available. Second, fix waistband articulation in report review. Not he reached for his waistband. Instead, hand position, what was or was not visible in the hand, lighting, distance, angle, prior warrant information, and what the movement resembled. A report that says the subject made a furtive movement gives a reviewing court nothing to work with. Third, command staff should read prong-two wins as notice that the conduct is now on the record and the next plaintiff will cite it.

cases.name: Harold v. Hagan
cases.decided: April 28, 2026 (panel opinion; rehearing petition pending as of the episode)
cases.topic: Canine apprehension of a prone, compliant, unarmed suspect, qualified immunity vacated
cases.caution: A petition for rehearing and rehearing en banc was filed in May 2026, and the current en banc posture could not be confirmed from a reliable source. Treat this panel opinion as instructive on where the Fourth Circuit is heading, not as settled law, and verify before citing it in testimony or in a policy revision. The source once rendered the name as Herald; Harold is used because it appears most often. The episode did not say whether this opinion is published.
cases.facts: Richard Harold broke into a car dealership in Chesterfield County, Virginia. Officers responded, including canine handler Louis Hagan. By the time Hagan and his dog, Kona, entered the storage room, Harold was on the floor in a submissive fetal position with his head down. He was unarmed. He was not resisting. Hagan signaled the dog to apprehend. The bite that followed was severe and prolonged, and it focused on areas of Harold's body that no controlled apprehension should reach. Harold sued. The transcript did not describe the district court ruling beyond the fact that the panel vacated qualified immunity. The episode covered the case briefly as a quick hit, because it presents the same warning and opportunity-to-comply question as the other three cases in a different tool.
cases.holding: A divided Fourth Circuit panel vacated qualified immunity. The court defined the right at issue as that of a non-threatening, unarmed, passively resisting suspect to be free from unnecessary, gratuitous, and disproportionate force by deployment of a police canine, and held that the right was clearly established. Unlike Searles and Foer, the panel reached the merits. The Fourth Circuit treated the dog as an instrument of significant force, consistent with earlier circuit law describing a police dog as functioning like another weapon. The panel opinion may not be final; a petition for rehearing and rehearing en banc was filed in May and its status is unconfirmed.
cases.dissent: Judge Richardson dissented. The transcript did not describe the grounds of the dissent.
cases.notDecided: The transcript did not describe the remaining claims or what happens on remand, and the en banc posture is unknown.
cases.inPractice: Deployment is a decision point, not a momentum event. The dog was staged, the room was breached, and the release followed; that sequence has its own gravity, and handlers have to be trained to interrupt it. The question at the threshold is not whether the deployment was planned but what the handler is looking at right now. A suspect who is prone, still, and compliant is not passively resisting in any sense that justifies a canine apprehension. If an officer would not strike this person with an impact weapon in this posture, he should not release a dog on him either.
cases.trainIt: Bite duration and target area are separate liability questions from the decision to deploy. Even a justified release becomes a problem if the call-off is slow or the apprehension lands somewhere it should not. Canine programs need documented call-off standards and a supervisory review that examines duration independently, not as an afterthought to the deployment decision. Before citing this case anywhere, pull the call-off standards and the deployment review form, confirm the en banc posture, and then decide whether the panel language changes the threshold for releasing on a prone subject.

sections.heading: California
sections.note: Nothing from this court in this episode. The episode reported no notable state high court force decision in the past seven days, and no California decision was discussed.

applications.title: Audit the Taser policy for a warning requirement and terrain contraindications
applications.body: Check whether policy requires a warning absent articulable exigency, and whether it addresses elevation, water, roadways, and stairs as deployment contraindications. If either is missing, Edwards v. Grubbs is the justification for adding it.

applications.title: Tell officers about the $21 million, and that it was personal
applications.body: The judgment was entered against the officer, not the city; the municipal verdict was set aside. Personal exposure is not a hypothetical in the Eleventh Circuit anymore.

applications.title: Fix waistband articulation in report review
applications.body: Sensory detail, not conclusions. Hand position, visibility, lighting, distance, angle, and prior information. The firearm in Searles was in the bag, and what matters is what the officer reasonably perceived and can describe.

applications.title: Treat every prong-two win as a countdown, not a clearance
applications.body: Searles and Foer were decided on the clearly established prong only, so the merits of both shootings remain open. The conduct is now published, and the next plaintiff has the citation the last one did not.

applications.title: Make the containment phase part of the narrative
applications.body: Foer rests on 30 minutes of ignored commands and attempted alternatives. If officers do not write that phase down, the agency cannot spend it later.

applications.title: Canine units: pull call-off standards before citing Harold
applications.body: Confirm the en banc posture first, then decide whether the panel language changes the threshold for releasing on a prone subject. Review bite duration independently of the decision to deploy.

quiz.q: In Edwards v. Grubbs, what fact did the Eleventh Circuit hang liability on?
options: The officer used a Taser in drive-stun mode
The officer fired in dart mode without any warning at an unarmed man fleeing on foot above a steep embankment
The officer failed to call for medical aid
The city had no Taser policy
quiz.teach: Deploying a Taser in dart mode without warning against an unarmed, non-dangerous suspect fleeing on foot in a highly dangerous location was held to be excessive force under clearly established law, and $21 million was left standing against the officer personally.

quiz.q: What did the Fifth Circuit decide in Searles v. City of Houston?
options: That the shooting was objectively reasonable
That the officer used excessive force but was immune
That no controlling authority or robust consensus placed the constitutional question beyond debate, so the officer was immune; the court did not decide whether the shooting was reasonable
That the city was liable for failure to train
quiz.teach: The panel resolved the case on the clearly established prong only. A prong-two win answers the liability question and leaves the tactical question untouched; qualified immunity is not a training standard.

quiz.q: In Foer v. City of Seattle, what made the final shot defensible according to the brief?
options: The officer gave a single warning immediately before firing
The documented 30-minute containment record of ignored commands and attempted alternatives, against a likely armed suspect who had already fired and was holding a child
The suspect fired at officers in the alley
The child had already been handed off to officers
quiz.teach: The containment period is not dead time. It is the record of every alternative attempted and every opportunity to comply refused, and no precedent addressed a fleeing, likely armed suspect who had already fired, held a child, and ignored commands for over half an hour.
